Section 1
Atlas 12-Week General Fitness Program is a fictional synthetic training guide created for dRAGn retrieval
demonstrations. It targets general strength, cardiovascular capacity, mobility, and consistency. It is not
medical advice.
Program design
 • Three strength sessions per week.
 • Two cardio sessions per week.
 • One active recovery session.
 • One full rest day.
 • Most strength sets finish with approximately 2–3 repetitions in reserve.
 The program prioritizes consistency and controlled progression. A participant should not force a planned

progression when technique, recovery, or symptoms indicate that the current workload is inappropriate.
Operational scenario
The weekly structure is intentionally distributed across the week. Monday, Wednesday, and Friday are
strength days; Tuesday and Saturday are cardio; Thursday is active recovery; Sunday is the full rest day. The
schedule is not a requirement to perform seven hard workouts. Adding another intense session on Thursday
can change the recovery balance and make the following strength session less productive.
Interpretation and operational notes
The weekly schedule should be interpreted as a workload distribution rather than seven mandatory hard

sessions. Monday, Wednesday, and Friday are strength days. Tuesday and Saturday are cardio days.
Thursday is intentionally recovery-oriented, and Sunday is the full rest day. Treating Thursday as another
strength session or adding unscheduled high-intensity work can change the intended recovery balance. This
distinction makes the guide useful for testing retrieval of schedule-specific conditions rather than simple
exercise-name matching.
Strength progression is conditional. The plan does not instruct the participant to add weight every week
regardless of performance. Load should increase only after the top of the prescribed repetition range is

completed with good technique for two sessions. If form deteriorates, recovery is poor, or symptoms occur,
maintaining or reducing the workload is more appropriate. This is a useful example of why an AI answer
should retrieve both the progression rule and the condition attached to it.
Cardio progression has its own conditions. Tuesday uses steady moderate aerobic work for 25–40 minutes.
Saturday intervals are introduced only after at least four weeks of consistent training, using six rounds of one
minute faster effort followed by two minutes easy. Weekly cardio duration should increase by no more than

approximately 10% when recovery is good. The plan therefore contains a time-based gate, a session
structure, and a progression ceiling that should not be conflated.
The guide treats recovery as part of training rather than as an optional afterthought. Sleep, hydration, food
intake, and manageable training volume affect readiness. Persistent decline in performance, unusually poor
sleep, or prolonged soreness are signals to reduce training volume rather than force progression. The safety
section also distinguishes ordinary fatigue from concerning symptoms such as sharp pain, fainting, unusual
shortness of breath, or sudden dizziness. These distinctions are important when generating grounded

Operational scenario
A participant who can complete all prescribed repetitions with good technique should progress gradually, but
the plan does not require an increase every week. Warm up for 5–8 minutes, use controlled range of motion,
and rest 90–150 seconds between demanding compound sets. Accessory work generally uses 45–90 seconds
of rest. If recovery or technique deteriorates, repeating the previous workload is preferable to forcing
progression.

2. Strength Training Rules
 • Begin with 5–8 minutes of general warm-up followed by movement-specific preparation.
 • Use controlled movement and consistent range of motion.
 • Rest 90–150 seconds between demanding compound sets and 45–90 seconds for accessory
 movements.
• Increase load by the smallest practical increment after completing the prescribed range with good
 technique for two sessions.
• Do not increase load when technique deteriorates or recovery is poor.
 
Readiness
Readiness can vary from session to session. The plan is a framework rather than a command to increase

load every week. A participant can repeat a workload when recovery is inadequate.
Operational scenario
Strength A emphasizes squat, push, row, hinge, and core patterns. A participant who cannot perform a full
push-up can use an incline variation without changing the purpose of the session. The Romanian deadlift
should remain a controlled hip hinge rather than a maximal lift. The dead bug is performed with controlled
trunk position. The goal is repeatable technique across sessions, not simply completing the largest possible
number of repetitions.

7. Mobility and Recovery
 • Thursday should leave the participant feeling better rather than exhausted.
 • Useful movements include ankle mobility, hip-flexor stretch, thoracic rotation, hamstring mobility, and
 shoulder range-of-motion drills.
• Sleep, hydration, and adequate food intake influence recovery and training performance.
 • Persistent decline in performance, unusually poor sleep, or prolonged soreness is a reason to reduce
 training volume.
Recovery checklist
 • Keep a consistent sleep schedule.
 • Hydrate according to climate, activity, body size, and sweat rate.

• Hydrate according to climate, activity, body size, and sweat rate.

Operational scenario
The 12-week structure starts with technique, moves into gradual overload, consolidates progress, and
finishes with a deload. During weeks 1–4 the emphasis is consistency and 2–3 repetitions in reserve. Weeks
5–8 emphasize gradual increases, weeks 9–11 consolidate, and week 12 reduces strength volume by
approximately 30–40%. Progression should follow performance rather than the calendar alone.

9. Nutrition, Substitutions and Safety
Nutrition
 • Distribute protein across meals rather than concentrating it in one meal.
 • Choose minimally processed foods, vegetables or fruit, whole-food carbohydrate sources, and
 protein-rich foods.
• Aggressive calorie restriction can reduce training performance and recovery.
 
Substitutions
 • Goblet squat → bodyweight squat or leg press.
 • Dumbbell row → resistance-band row.
 • Lat pulldown → resistance-band pulldown.
 • Dumbbell bench press → push-up or incline push-up.
 
Safety
 • Stop for sharp pain, sudden dizziness, fainting, unusual shortness of breath, or another concerning

symptom.
• People with medical conditions, recent injuries, pregnancy, or significant limitations should obtain
 appropriate professional guidance before starting.
Operational scenario
The program is a general fitness guide, not medical advice. Sharp pain, sudden dizziness, fainting, unusual
shortness of breath, or another concerning symptom is a reason to stop and seek appropriate professional
guidance. People with medical conditions, recent injuries, pregnancy, or significant limitations should obtain
suitable advice before starting. Consistency, controlled progression, and recovery are more important than
forcing a planned workload.
